messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At thirty-eight, Mai had spent more than a decade as a welder, her hands steady and her eye precise, working in a fabrication shop outside Portland. The accident happened on a Tuesday afternoon. She was welding a steel beam, her visor down, the arc hissing and spitting. A coworker named Tom stepped into her work zone without warning—she never heard him approach. When she turned, the torch followed, and the flame caught the sleeve of his flannel shirt. The fabric ignited instantly. She remembered the sound of his scream, the smell of burning cotton and skin, and then a taste in her mouth—sharp, metallic, like hot copper and smoke, a taste that would return without warning in the months that followed, coating her tongue even when she was nowhere near a shop.

What happened next was fragmented. She recalled dropping the torch, pulling off her gloves, shouting. But the few seconds between the flame catching and Tom collapsing on the concrete floor were missing, a blank space she could not fill no matter how many times she tried. She knew she had dialed 911. She knew she had knelt beside him, his burns already blistering, and that her hands had been shaking so badly she could barely press a towel to his arm. But the sequence was wrong, the details scattered, and that incomplete picture haunted her more than the parts she could see. Every time the memory surfaced, guilt flooded through her chest like a wave—hot, suffocating, absolute. She had done this. She had turned without looking, without warning. She had known better.

In the weeks after, Mai tried to push the event out of her mind. She avoided thinking about it deliberately, filling her days with mechanical tasks—cleaning her apartment, organizing drawers—anything to keep her thoughts busy. But the rumination slipped in anyway, especially at night. Lying awake, she would replay the moment over and over, searching for what she had done wrong. Why hadn't she checked her blind spot? Why hadn't she called out that she was about to move? She dwelled on every mistake, turning them over like stones in her hands, each one heavier than the last. Sleep became a war. She would drift off only to jolt awake with the taste in her mouth, her heart hammering, the bedroom dark and silent but her body convinced she was back in the shop.

She stopped going to work. At first she told her supervisor she needed a few days, then a week, then she simply stopped answering the phone. The shop was full of people she had worked with for years, but she could not face them. She was certain that if she walked in, everyone would be staring at her, that they all knew exactly what she had done—and worse, that they were right to judge her. Avoidance spread beyond the shop. She stopped seeing friends, stopped returning calls from her mother, who lived three states away. When she had to go to the grocery store, she chose late hours when the aisles were empty, and if she saw anyone she vaguely recognized, she ducked into another aisle or left without buying anything. She had come to believe that being around people was dangerous—not because they might hurt her, but because she might hurt them. What frightened her most was the possibility that she was fundamentally careless, that the accident had revealed something true about her that she could not undo.

Concentration became a problem. She would start a task—folding laundry, paying a bill—and find herself staring at the same point for ten minutes, the guilt so loud in her head that she could not follow a single thought through to completion. Physical reactions came without warning: a gust of wind from a passing truck could make her flinch and start sweating; the hiss of a steam radiator sent her pulse racing. She had not touched her welding equipment since the accident, and she could not even enter the garage of her apartment building because the smell of oil and metal triggered a cascade of sensations—the heat of the torch, the taste, the scream.

By the time she finally called a therapist, she had been unemployed for four months, her savings nearly gone, and her isolation so complete that she had not spoken to another person face-to-face in over two weeks. She said she did not know if she wanted to feel better—she was not sure she deserved to—but she could not keep living with the taste in her mouth and the missing seconds and the weight of what she had done. She was terrified that talking about it would only make the memories sharper, more real, but she was more terrified of staying like this: a woman who had once built things, now unable to hold anything steady.
